    Forward model¶

    This example walks through the pieces of a pwdsim forward simulation: defining the track, defining the car, and simulating a run down the track. So far only the track is implemented.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch

import pwdsim
from pwdsim.plotting import plot_car, plot_energy, plot_run, plot_runs, plot_track
from pwdsim.units import DEGREE, FOOT, GRAM, INCH, OUNCE
    import warnings import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import torch import pwdsim from pwdsim.plotting import plot_car, plot_energy, plot_run, plot_runs, plot_track from pwdsim.units import DEGREE, FOOT, GRAM, INCH, OUNCE

    The track¶

    pwdsim describes a track by its angle from the horizontal, $\theta(s)$, as a function of arc length $s$ along the path of the wheel contacts. The curvature is $\kappa = \theta'$, and the track profile comes from integrating $x' = \cos\theta$ and $y' = \sin\theta$.

    Our standard track approximates a 42 ft BestTrack aluminum track, one of the most common commercial tracks. From the manufacturer's FAQ and specifications:

    • the curve section is 41 in long with a smooth 48 in radius,
    • after the curve come four 84 in straight sections and a 40 in stop section,
    • the start pin is about 37 ft 9 in from the end of the track,
    • the racing distance from the start pin to the timer is 442 in, and
    • the starting gate is approximately 4 ft from the floor.

    Treating the whole curve section as a circular arc gives a ramp angle of $41/48$ rad, about 49 degrees. Short easement curves join the arc to the straight sections so that the curvature changes smoothly.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    track = pwdsim.besttrack(42)

print(f"Track length:        {track.length / FOOT:.1f} ft")
print(f"Start pin:           {track.s_start / INCH:.1f} in from the top")
print(f"Racing distance:     {(track.s_finish - track.s_start) / INCH:.1f} in")
print(f"Ramp angle:          {-track.angle(0.0) / DEGREE:.1f} deg")
print(f"Height at start pin: {track.height(track.s_start) / INCH:.1f} in")
    track = pwdsim.besttrack(42) print(f"Track length: {track.length / FOOT:.1f} ft") print(f"Start pin: {track.s_start / INCH:.1f} in from the top") print(f"Racing distance: {(track.s_finish - track.s_start) / INCH:.1f} in") print(f"Ramp angle: {-track.angle(0.0) / DEGREE:.1f} deg") print(f"Height at start pin: {track.height(track.s_start) / INCH:.1f} in")
    Track length:        42.0 ft
Start pin:           51.0 in from the top
Racing distance:     442.0 in
Ramp angle:          48.9 deg
Height at start pin: 44.0 in

    The start pin sits about 44 in above the flat part of the track. That matches the quoted 4 ft gate height if the flat sections stand a few inches off the floor.

    The profile below exaggerates the vertical scale. The angle and curvature along the track show the straight ramp, the curve, and the flat run.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    fig = plot_track(track, unit="ft")
plt.show()
    fig = plot_track(track, unit="ft") plt.show()

    Zooming in on the curve, at true scale, shows the easements where the curvature ramps up to $1/R$ over one inch of track at each end of the circular arc.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    s_curve = track.knots[[1, 4]]
x_curve, y_curve = track.position(s_curve)
s_curve, x_curve, y_curve = (v.numpy() for v in (s_curve, x_curve, y_curve))
margin = 6 * INCH

fig = plot_track(track, unit="in", equal_aspect=True)
ax_profile, ax_angle = fig.axes[:2]
ax_profile.set_xlim((x_curve[0] - margin) / INCH, (x_curve[1] + margin) / INCH)
ax_profile.set_ylim((y_curve[1] - margin) / INCH, (y_curve[0] + margin) / INCH)
ax_angle.set_xlim((s_curve[0] - margin) / INCH, (s_curve[1] + margin) / INCH)
plt.show()
    s_curve = track.knots[[1, 4]] x_curve, y_curve = track.position(s_curve) s_curve, x_curve, y_curve = (v.numpy() for v in (s_curve, x_curve, y_curve)) margin = 6 * INCH fig = plot_track(track, unit="in", equal_aspect=True) ax_profile, ax_angle = fig.axes[:2] ax_profile.set_xlim((x_curve[0] - margin) / INCH, (x_curve[1] + margin) / INCH) ax_profile.set_ylim((y_curve[1] - margin) / INCH, (y_curve[0] + margin) / INCH) ax_angle.set_xlim((s_curve[0] - margin) / INCH, (s_curve[1] + margin) / INCH) plt.show()

    The car¶

    The simulator needs a handful of essential car properties: the mass and its distribution, the axle and wheel geometry, and the friction and drag coefficients. SimpleCar takes these values directly and stores each one as a trainable torch parameter. The Cars page of the docs describes the car model in detail.

    The values below describe a legal, reasonably well-built car made from the standard BSA kit. They are estimates, mostly from the Wikibooks derby physics page:

    • Geometry: the kit's axle slots are about $4\tfrac{3}{8}$ in apart, with the rear slot about $\tfrac{7}{8}$ in from the back of the 7 in block.
    • Mass: the 5 oz limit, with the center of gravity 1 in ahead of the rear axle, a common target for fast cars. The body's pitching inertia is estimated as a uniform 7 in by 1.25 in block, $I_b \approx M (l^2 + h^2) / 12$.
    • Wheels: 95.0 mm around, so a radius of 0.595 in, weighing 2.6 g each with $I \approx 0.58\, m r^2$. The axles are 0.087 in in diameter.
    • Friction and drag: a lubricated axle friction coefficient of 0.1, a rolling resistance coefficient of 0.002, a drag coefficient of 0.4, and the $0.0014\ \mathrm{m}^2$ frontal area of an uncut block.
    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    mass = 5 * OUNCE
wheel_radius = 0.595 * INCH
wheel_inertia = 0.58 * (2.6 * GRAM) * wheel_radius**2
body_inertia = mass * ((7 * INCH) ** 2 + (1.25 * INCH) ** 2) / 12

car_args = dict(
    cg=(1.0 * INCH, 0.4 * INCH),
    wheelbase=4.375 * INCH,
    front_offset=(7 - 0.875) * INCH,
    mass=mass,
    body_inertia=body_inertia,
    rear_wheel_inertia=wheel_inertia,
    front_wheel_inertia=wheel_inertia,
    rear_wheel_radius=wheel_radius,
    front_wheel_radius=wheel_radius,
    rear_axle_radius=0.087 / 2 * INCH,
    front_axle_radius=0.087 / 2 * INCH,
    rear_axle_friction=0.1,
    front_axle_friction=0.1,
    frontal_area=0.0014,
    drag_coefficient=0.4,
    rolling_friction=0.002,
)
car = pwdsim.SimpleCar(**car_args)

for name, value in car.summary().items():
    values = value if isinstance(value, list) else [value]
    print(f"{name:20s}", *(f"{v:.4g}" for v in values))
    mass = 5 * OUNCE wheel_radius = 0.595 * INCH wheel_inertia = 0.58 * (2.6 * GRAM) * wheel_radius**2 body_inertia = mass * ((7 * INCH) ** 2 + (1.25 * INCH) ** 2) / 12 car_args = dict( cg=(1.0 * INCH, 0.4 * INCH), wheelbase=4.375 * INCH, front_offset=(7 - 0.875) * INCH, mass=mass, body_inertia=body_inertia, rear_wheel_inertia=wheel_inertia, front_wheel_inertia=wheel_inertia, rear_wheel_radius=wheel_radius, front_wheel_radius=wheel_radius, rear_axle_radius=0.087 / 2 * INCH, front_axle_radius=0.087 / 2 * INCH, rear_axle_friction=0.1, front_axle_friction=0.1, frontal_area=0.0014, drag_coefficient=0.4, rolling_friction=0.002, ) car = pwdsim.SimpleCar(**car_args) for name, value in car.summary().items(): values = value if isinstance(value, list) else [value] print(f"{name:20s}", *(f"{v:.4g}" for v in values))

body_inertia         0.0003853
n_rear_wheels        2

    All values are in SI units. Every property except the wheel counts is a trainable parameter, ready for a torch optimizer:

    Simulating a run¶

    A Simulation puts the car on the track, with the front of the car against the start pin, and integrates its equation of motion in time. The equation of motion is assembled from modular physics terms, and by default a simulation uses all of them:

    Term Physics
    gravity potential energy of the car, $M g\, y_g$
    translation kinetic energy of the car moving with its center of gravity
    body_rotation kinetic energy of the car body pitching through the curve
    wheel_spin kinetic energy of the spinning wheels, rolling without slip
    drag aerodynamic drag, $\tfrac{1}{2} \rho C_d A v^2$
    axle_friction friction between the wheels and axles, a torque $\mu N a$
    rolling_friction rolling resistance of the wheels, a force $c_r N$

    The simulation uses backward Euler time steps of 0.1 ms.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    sim = pwdsim.Simulation(track, car)
print("Physics terms:", list(sim.physics))

run = sim()
print(f"Finish time:  {run.finish_time.item():.4f} s")
print(f"Finish speed: {run.finish_speed.item():.3f} m/s")
print(f"Max speed:    {run.max_speed.item():.3f} m/s")
print(f"Min normal forces (rear, front): {run.min_normal_force.detach().numpy()} N")
    sim = pwdsim.Simulation(track, car) print("Physics terms:", list(sim.physics)) run = sim() print(f"Finish time: {run.finish_time.item():.4f} s") print(f"Finish speed: {run.finish_speed.item():.3f} m/s") print(f"Max speed: {run.max_speed.item():.3f} m/s") print(f"Min normal forces (rear, front): {run.min_normal_force.detach().numpy()} N")
    Physics terms: ['gravity', 'translation', 'body_rotation', 'wheel_spin', 'drag', 'axle_friction', 'rolling_friction']

    Finish time:  2.7848 s

    Finish speed: 4.419 m/s
Max speed:    4.688 m/s

    Min normal forces (rear, front): [0.60111821 0.18889147] N

    The car speeds up down the ramp and through the curve, reaching its top speed as it enters the flat run, where friction and drag slowly bleed off speed. The normal forces jump up in the curve, where the track has to turn the car's momentum upwards. If either normal force went negative, the simulation would warn that a wheel lifted off the track.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    fig = plot_run(run, unit="ft")
plt.show()
    fig = plot_run(run, unit="ft") plt.show()

    Here's the car at true scale as it goes through the curve. The car pitches up as it follows the track, and the wheels ride one radius off the track surface.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    fig = plot_car(sim, torch.tensor([75, 90, 105, 120, 135]) * INCH)
plt.show()
    fig = plot_car(sim, torch.tensor([75, 90, 105, 120, 135]) * INCH) plt.show()

    Simple vs. full physics¶

    How much does each piece of physics matter? The simple physics has only gravity and the translational kinetic energy: a car rolling without friction or drag, with no rotational inertia. Here is the same car with the simple and the full physics.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    simple_run = pwdsim.Simulation(track, car, physics=pwdsim.simple_physics())()

for label, r in (("simple", simple_run), ("full", run)):
    print(
        f"{label:>6}: finish {r.finish_time.item():.4f} s, "
        f"finish speed {r.finish_speed.item():.3f} m/s, "
        f"max speed {r.max_speed.item():.3f} m/s"
    )

fig = plot_runs([simple_run, run], labels=["simple", "full"], unit="ft")
plt.show()
    simple_run = pwdsim.Simulation(track, car, physics=pwdsim.simple_physics())() for label, r in (("simple", simple_run), ("full", run)): print( f"{label:>6}: finish {r.finish_time.item():.4f} s, " f"finish speed {r.finish_speed.item():.3f} m/s, " f"max speed {r.max_speed.item():.3f} m/s" ) fig = plot_runs([simple_run, run], labels=["simple", "full"], unit="ft") plt.show()
    simple: finish 2.6352 s, finish speed 4.865 m/s, max speed 4.865 m/s

      full: finish 2.7848 s, finish speed 4.419 m/s, max speed 4.688 m/s

    With the full physics, part of the car's potential energy goes into spinning the wheels and pitching the body, and drag and friction steadily dissipate energy. The energy budget shows where it goes; the total of the mechanical and dissipated energy stays constant.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    fig = plot_energy(run)
plt.show()
    fig = plot_energy(run) plt.show()

    To see what each term costs, switch it off and race again. Each row is the time the car would save without that piece of physics. The which physics matters? example looks at this in more detail.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    with torch.no_grad():
    full_time = run.finish_time.item()
    for name in list(sim.physics)[2:]:
        sim.disable(name)
        saved = full_time - sim().finish_time.item()
        sim.enable(name)
        print(f"{name:>16}: {saved * 1000:5.1f} ms")
    with torch.no_grad(): full_time = run.finish_time.item() for name in list(sim.physics)[2:]: sim.disable(name) saved = full_time - sim().finish_time.item() sim.enable(name) print(f"{name:>16}: {saved * 1000:5.1f} ms")
       body_rotation:   0.2 ms

          wheel_spin:  55.7 ms

                drag:  27.9 ms

       axle_friction:  53.6 ms

    rolling_friction:  15.1 ms

    Sensitivities¶

    The finish time is differentiable with respect to every car parameter. The adjoint method provides the gradients at about the cost of one more simulation.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    run.finish_time.backward()
dt_dcg = car.cg_.grad * INCH * 1000
print(f"Moving the CG forward 1 in:     {dt_dcg[0].item():+.1f} ms")
print(f"Moving the CG up 1 in:          {dt_dcg[1].item():+.1f} ms")
print(f"Adding 1 oz:                    {car.mass_.grad.item() * OUNCE * 1000:+.1f} ms")
print(
    "Axle friction coefficient +0.01: "
    f"{(car.rear_axle_friction_.grad + car.front_axle_friction_.grad).item() * 10:+.1f}"
    " ms"
)
    run.finish_time.backward() dt_dcg = car.cg_.grad * INCH * 1000 print(f"Moving the CG forward 1 in: {dt_dcg[0].item():+.1f} ms") print(f"Moving the CG up 1 in: {dt_dcg[1].item():+.1f} ms") print(f"Adding 1 oz: {car.mass_.grad.item() * OUNCE * 1000:+.1f} ms") print( "Axle friction coefficient +0.01: " f"{(car.rear_axle_friction_.grad + car.front_axle_friction_.grad).item() * 10:+.1f}" " ms" )
    Moving the CG forward 1 in:     +17.7 ms
Moving the CG up 1 in:          +3.7 ms
Adding 1 oz:                    -16.7 ms
Axle friction coefficient +0.01: +5.6 ms

    What matters most is how far the center of gravity drops between the start and the flat run. Moving the center of gravity back raises it on the ramp, where the car is tilted, but not on the flat, so it drops further and the car is faster. Raising the center of gravity does the opposite: on the ramp a point 1 in above the axles is only $\cos 49^\circ \approx 0.66$ in higher, while on the flat it is the full inch higher, so the drop gets smaller.

    With the simple physics the mass doesn't matter at all, since every force is proportional to it. With the full physics a heavier car is faster: friction still scales with the weight, but drag and the rotational inertia of the wheels don't, so they slow a heavy car less.

    Comparing designs¶

    Car properties can have a batch dimension to simulate several designs in one run. Here we sweep the center of gravity from right over the rear axle to 2 in ahead of it, and look at both the finish time and the smallest normal force on the front wheels.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    cg_along = torch.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 9) * INCH
cg_sweep = torch.stack([cg_along, torch.full_like(cg_along, 0.4 * INCH)], dim=-1)
cars = pwdsim.SimpleCar(**(car_args | {"cg": cg_sweep}))

with torch.no_grad(), warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    sweep = pwdsim.Simulation(track, cars)()
    finish_times = sweep.finish_time
    min_front_force = sweep.min_normal_force[:, 1]
for warning in caught:
    print(f"{warning.category.__name__}: {warning.message}")

lifted = min_front_force < 0
fig, (ax_time, ax_force) = plt.subplots(
    2, 1, figsize=(8, 6), sharex=True, constrained_layout=True
)
ax_time.plot(cg_along / INCH, finish_times * 1000, "o-")
ax_time.plot(cg_along[lifted] / INCH, finish_times[lifted] * 1000, "rx", ms=10)
ax_time.set_ylabel("finish time (ms)")
ax_force.plot(cg_along / INCH, min_front_force, "o-")
ax_force.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
ax_force.set_xlabel("center of gravity ahead of the rear axle (in)")
ax_force.set_ylabel("min front normal force (N)")
plt.show()
    cg_along = torch.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 9) * INCH cg_sweep = torch.stack([cg_along, torch.full_like(cg_along, 0.4 * INCH)], dim=-1) cars = pwdsim.SimpleCar(**(car_args | {"cg": cg_sweep})) with torch.no_grad(), warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: warnings.simplefilter("always") sweep = pwdsim.Simulation(track, cars)() finish_times = sweep.finish_time min_front_force = sweep.min_normal_force[:, 1] for warning in caught: print(f"{warning.category.__name__}: {warning.message}") lifted = min_front_force < 0 fig, (ax_time, ax_force) = plt.subplots( 2, 1, figsize=(8, 6), sharex=True, constrained_layout=True ) ax_time.plot(cg_along / INCH, finish_times * 1000, "o-") ax_time.plot(cg_along[lifted] / INCH, finish_times[lifted] * 1000, "rx", ms=10) ax_time.set_ylabel("finish time (ms)") ax_force.plot(cg_along / INCH, min_front_force, "o-") ax_force.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8) ax_force.set_xlabel("center of gravity ahead of the rear axle (in)") ax_force.set_ylabel("min front normal force (N)") plt.show()
    LiftOffWarning: A wheel lifted off the track (negative normal force) before the finish; the results are not physical

    Moving the center of gravity back keeps paying off, but only up to a point. As the car comes out of the curve it stops pitching up, and stopping the rotation of the car body takes a torque that unloads the front wheels. With the center of gravity much closer than about 3/4 in to the rear axle, the front normal force goes negative (red crosses): the front wheels would lift off the track, which the model doesn't allow. The simulation warns about this, and reports the minimum normal forces so an optimizer can avoid these designs.

    How far forward the limit sits depends on the pitching moment of inertia of the body, $I_b$, which here is a rough estimate.
